newsitem.title: CANADA: Quebec again dominates Canada election campaign.
newsitem.headline: Quebec again dominates Canada election campaign.

text.p: The touchy issue of Quebec possibly leaving Canada has catapulted to the top of the federal election campaign as separatists restate their goal of a sovereign country while federalists scrap among themselves.

Canada came within a percentage point of falling apart in a 1995 referendum on Quebec sovereignty, and though politicians danced around the issue in the first week of the current campaign, they have finally had to face it head on.
"It's a bitter fight," commented University of Ottawa political scientist Clinton Archibald.
Prime Minister Jean Chretien, a francophone Quebecker himself, called the election, an important one for Quebec, on April 27.

The June 2 election will determine whether the Bloc Quebecois will remain the official opposition in Parliament, with a platform to promote its separatist ambitions. It will help determine how well other parties do in Quebec and the rest of Canada, and which vision of dealing with Quebec will prevail.

The western-based Reform Party had been pressing the issue hardest, its leader Preston Manning railing against Chretien for trying to write into the Constitution that Quebec is a "distinct society" -- which the party says is a code word for allowing Quebec to get special treatment.

Reform, advocating devolution of power to all provinces to help satisfy Quebec's desire for more power, has been running ads on the issue exclusively in British Columbia, where it thinks feelings run strongest against a "distinct society."
Chretien lashed out at Manning on his home turf in Calgary on Tuesday: "Preston Manning said I am old. Well, I'm old enough to know just how divisive and how irresponsible his brand of politics is."

Conservative leader Jean Charest, one of the most eloquent spokesmen for Canadian unity during the referendum campaign, slammed what has become known as the federal government's Plan B -- a strategy to deal with a vote in favour of sovereignty.

"As prime minister of Canada, I do not anticipate the dissolution of the country. I don't intend to invent a Plan B. Canada is not a B country," he told a news conference in Quebec City on Wednesday. Instead he advocated reconciliation, partnership and co-management with the provinces.

The Bloc ran a disastrous first campaign week, displaying divisions within the movement and making errors like showing its leader Gilles Duceppe with a hairnet at a cheese factory and sending a media bus in the wrong direction.
Duceppe did not stress sovereignty in that first week, despite the fact that this is the thread holding the party together, but this week he has come out swinging.
He referred to sovereignty more than 10 times during an unusually energetic speech to businessmen on Tuesday in a Quebec City suburb, where he received a standing ovation.
"I have a dream of a sovereign Quebec. I have a dream of a sovereign country," he thundered.

A Reuters poll which put Chretien's Liberals more than 30 points ahead of both the Conservatives and Reform nationally gave the Liberals 42.9 percent in Quebec to the Bloc's 31.3 percent and the Conservatives 14.0 percent.

The poll, conducted May 1 to 4, had a 3.2 percentage point margin of error nationally but a higher margin in each region. Other polls taken before the campaign have also shown slippage from the Bloc's 49 percent showing in the 1993 elections.

In Quebec as in the rest of the country, the unity issue evokes visceral reactions cutting both ways, as some say too much has been done for the mainly French-speaking province and others worrying that the government needs to do more.
For 18 of the last 19 years, Canada's prime ministers have been from Quebec, and that could affect even Charest outside the province while helping him at home.

"I would be very uncomfortable, even though my leanings are towards the Conservatives, voting for a Quebecker whose background is French. It would appear as if you are voting for more concessions for Quebec," Ontario voter Allyn Heyes told Reuters.
